ecosystem.comment: CPython library published to PyPI, requires-python >=3.9 with classifiers through 3.14. No other runtime is targeted.

license.comment: MIT per the GitHub licence metadata and the pyproject [project] license field.

implementation.comment: HMAC uses the standard library's hmac/hashlib. Every asymmetric algorithm (RS/PS/ES/EdDSA) is delegated to the optional `cryptography` package, which binds OpenSSL — hence both tags. Base `pip install PyJWT` ships HS* and `none` only; `pip install PyJWT[crypto]` enables the rest.

package.comment: PyPI distribution name PyJWT; import name is `jwt`.

documentation.comment: The README points at readthedocs as the full documentation; the usage page is the task-oriented guide and there is a separate API reference.

first-release.comment: Earliest release on PyPI is 0.1.1, uploaded 2011-02-24.

latest-version.comment: 2.13.0 released 2026-05-21; still pre-3.0 but with a long-stable 2.x API. Checked 2026-07-30.

hmac-hs.comment: Registered in get_default_algorithms() via HMACAlgorithm; available in the base install with no optional dependency.

rsa-pkcs1.comment: RSAAlgorithm; requires the `crypto` extra (`cryptography`), otherwise the algorithm is not registered.

ecdsa.comment: ECAlgorithm registers ES256, ES256K (secp256k1, RFC 8812), ES384 and ES512 — plus a legacy `ES521` alias for the same P-521 curve. Requires the `crypto` extra. Curve/alg binding is enforced per RFC 7518 §3.4 since 2.11.0.

eddsa.comment: One registered identifier, `EdDSA` (RFC 8037), whose OKPAlgorithm accepts both Ed25519 and Ed448 keys; the test fixture set contains jwk_okp_key_Ed25519.json and jwk_okp_key_Ed448.json. The curve-specific `Ed25519` alg identifier is not registered. Requires the `crypto` extra.

jwe-key-management.comment: PyJWT implements JWS/JWT only — the package contains api_jws, api_jwt, api_jwk and jwks_client modules and no JWE module at all.

jwe-content-encryption.comment: No JWE support, so no content-encryption algorithms.

deprecated-algorithms-available.comment: `none` is a registered algorithm (NoneAlgorithm) reachable only by explicitly listing it in `algorithms=["none"]` with an empty key. RSA keys under 2048 bits still work: since 2.11.0 they raise an InsecureKeyLengthWarning but are only rejected when `enforce_minimum_key_length=True` is passed. ES256K is registered as its own RFC 8812 identifier, not as an unrestricted secp256k1 under ES256.

algorithm-extensibility.comment: PyJWS.register_algorithm(alg_id, alg_obj) / unregister_algorithm() accept any Algorithm subclass and are exported as jwt.register_algorithm. This also lets a caller replace or re-add algorithms the library deliberately restricts, so it is an escape hatch around its own checks.

rejects-alg-none.comment: Verified in 2.13.0. decode() raises DecodeError ("It is required that you pass in a value for the 'algorithms' argument") when verify_signature is on and no algorithm list is given, and the header `alg` must appear in that list, so `none` only verifies if the caller literally writes algorithms=["none"]. NoneAlgorithm.prepare_key additionally raises InvalidKeyError unless the key is empty/None.

algorithm-pinning.comment: The normal path forces an explicit allow-list: `algorithms` is mandatory whenever the key is not a PyJWK. When a PyJWK (e.g. from PyJWKClient) is passed, the algorithm is taken from the key's `alg`/kty-derived algorithm_name instead — and since 2.13.0 the token header `alg` is bound to PyJWK.algorithm_name, closing the allow-list bypass of CVE-2026-48523.

algorithm-confusion-resistance.comment: Guideline level 3: keys are plain str/bytes or cryptography objects, and confusion is prevented by runtime blocklists that only bite once the caller has supplied an algorithm list. HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key rejects PEM/OpenSSH/x509 material ("asymmetric key or x509 certificate ... should not be used as an HMAC secret") and, since 2.13.0, raw JWK JSON documents. This is a defence added after the fact: CVE-2017-11424 and CVE-2022-29217 were key-confusion bugs, and CVE-2026-48526 (high, fixed 2.13.0) was the same class again via a JWK-as-HMAC-secret.

unverified-decode-separated.comment: Headers have a distinct API (jwt.get_unverified_header), but reading claims without verification is the same jwt.decode() call with options={"verify_signature": False} — a flag on the normal path, which the attribute definition scores as false. The docs call the practice "generally ill-advised".

default-claim-validation.comment: Default options are verify_signature/verify_exp/verify_nbf/verify_iat/verify_aud/verify_iss/verify_sub/verify_jti all True with require=[]. In practice exp, nbf and iat are checked whenever present. `aud` fails closed: if the token carries an aud claim and the caller passed no audience, _validate_aud raises InvalidAudienceError. `iss`, `sub` and `jti` checks return early unless the corresponding expected value is passed, so they are not tagged. Absent claims are never required unless listed in `require`.

audience-issuer-required.comment: `audience` and `issuer` are optional keyword arguments defaulting to None; a token with no aud/iss claim verifies happily without them. Partial credit: a token that does carry `aud` is rejected when the caller supplied no audience, and `options={"require": ["aud", "iss"]}` can force presence — but nothing in the API forces the caller to state expectations.

clock-skew-configurable.comment: decode(..., leeway=...) accepts seconds as a float or a datetime.timedelta and applies to exp, nbf and iat. Default is 0 — no implicit skew allowance.

constant-time-comparison.comment: HMACAlgorithm.verify returns hmac.compare_digest(sig, self.sign(msg, key)) — the standard library's constant-time primitive. Asymmetric verification is delegated to `cryptography`.

minimum-key-size-enforced.comment: The checks exist (RSA _MIN_KEY_SIZE = 2048 bits, HMAC secret at least the hash digest size, per RFC 7518 §3.2) but are advisory by default: 2.11.0 introduced them as an InsecureKeyLengthWarning and they only raise InvalidKeyError when the caller opts in with `enforce_minimum_key_length=True`, which defaults to False in the options dict. Recorded false because the default path does not reject. Empty HMAC keys are rejected outright since 2.13.0.

crit-header-handling.comment: As of 2.12.0, _validate_crit runs on decode with _supported_crit = {"b64"}: crit must be a non-empty list of strings, every entry must be present in the header, and any extension outside the supported set is rejected. This is recent — up to and including 2.11.0 unknown crit entries were accepted (CVE-2026-32597, high, fixed in 2.12.0).

nested-depth-limits.comment: Not applicable in the JWE/PBES2 sense — PyJWT has no JWE and no nested-token handling, so there is no recursion to bound and no p2c cap to set. The one related DoS was CVE-2026-48525 (unbounded Base64URL decoding of the unused payload segment of a b64=false detached JWS), fixed in 2.13.0 by not decoding that segment rather than by adding a size limit. Left null rather than forcing a true/false.

cve-history.comment: Nine GitHub advisories as of 2026-07-30, all patched. CVE-2017-11424 (key confusion, GHSA-r9jw-mwhq-wp62); CVE-2022-29217 (key confusion via non-blocklisted public key formats, high, fixed 2.4.0); CVE-2024-53861 (partial iss matching, low, fixed 2.10.1); CVE-2026-32597 (unknown `crit` extensions accepted, high, fixed 2.12.0); and a batch of five published 2026-06-15 all fixed in 2.13.0 — CVE-2026-48526 (public-key JWK accepted as HMAC secret, high), CVE-2026-48523 (algorithm allow-list bypass via PyJWK/PyJWKClient, medium), CVE-2026-48522 (PyJWKClient missing URL scheme allow-list, SSRF/file:// token forgery, medium), CVE-2026-48525 (b64=false detached-JWS decoding DoS, medium), CVE-2026-48524 (unbounded JWKS refetch via attacker-controlled kid, low). Read as a track record: recurring algorithm-confusion class, but consistently fixed and disclosed through GitHub advisories. Anything older than 2.13.0 should be considered vulnerable to a high-severity forgery.

security-policy.comment: SECURITY.md directs reporters to GitHub's private "Report a vulnerability" workflow, with security@jpadilla.com as a fallback. The supported-versions table is stale — it still names 2.10.x as the supported line while 2.13.0 is current.

independent-security-review.comment: Searched for a published third-party audit and found none. What exists is coordinated individual disclosure: the 2026 advisory batch was reported by external researchers (GHSA-xgmm-8j9v-c9wx credits reporter aradona91) and triaged via GitHub advisories — valuable, but not an audit.

jws.comment: Both directions: PyJWS.encode/decode plus the JWT layer on top (jwt.encode / jwt.decode).

jwe.comment: No JWE implementation of any kind — the package is JWS/JWT only. Users needing JWE reach for joserfc or Authlib.

jwk-parsing.comment: PyJWK / PyJWK.from_json / PyJWKSet parse individual keys and key sets; each Algorithm implements from_jwk and to_jwk for oct, RSA, EC and OKP key types.

jwks-remote-fetch.comment: PyJWKClient(uri) fetches the key set itself over urllib, with configurable headers, timeout (default 30s) and ssl_context. Since 2.13.0 the URI is restricted to http/https schemes (CVE-2026-48522).

jwks-caching-rotation.comment: cache_jwk_set defaults to True with a lifespan of 300 seconds (TTL only — no Cache-Control parsing), plus an optional per-key LRU (cache_keys, max_cached_keys=16). On an unknown kid the client refetches once and retries. There is no rate limiting beyond the TTL, which is exactly the amplification vector of CVE-2026-48524; the TTL-based cache is the mitigation.

kid-selection.comment: PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt reads `kid` from the unverified header and looks it up in the key set; PyJWKSet supports jwk_set[kid] lookup directly.

jwk-thumbprint.comment: No RFC 7638 thumbprint computation anywhere in api_jwk.py — PyJWK exposes only kty, kid and use. RFC 9278 thumbprint URIs likewise absent.

nested-jwt.comment: Requires JWE, which PyJWT does not implement.

json-serialization.comment: Compact serialization only; api_jws builds and splits `header.payload.signature` strings and has no flattened/general JSON or multi-signature support.

detached-payload.comment: RFC 7515 Appendix F both ways: encode(..., is_payload_detached=True) and decode(..., detached_payload=b"..."). Not documented on the readthedocs usage page. The feature carried CVE-2026-48525 (DoS) until 2.13.0.

unencoded-payload.comment: RFC 7797 `b64: false` is handled on both encode and decode, and `b64` is the single member of the supported `crit` set. 2.13.0 tightened the handling to match RFC 7515 Appendix F.

key-generation.comment: No generation helpers — algorithms only prepare, sign, verify and convert existing keys. Users generate keys with `cryptography` or openssl and hand them in.

x509-header-support.comment: None of x5c, x5t, x5t#S256 or x5u is read or validated: PyJWK exposes only kty/kid/use and no certificate chain handling exists. (X.509 material is recognised in one place only — HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key rejects PEM certificates as HMAC secrets.)

key-input-formats.comment: prepare_key accepts PEM (loaded via cryptography's load_pem_private_key/load_pem_public_key, so PKCS#1, PKCS#8 and SPKI bodies all work), OpenSSH public keys (`ssh-` prefix — no tag for this), already-constructed cryptography key objects, and raw bytes/str for HMAC. JWK and JWK Set documents go through PyJWK/PyJWKSet. No DER, PKCS#12 or keystore ingestion.

external-signer-support.comment: No signer abstraction: encode() takes key material and calls the algorithm object directly. A KMS/HSM signer can only be bolted on by subclassing Algorithm and calling register_algorithm, which is an extensibility hook rather than a supported external-signer interface.

framework-integrations.comment: No first-party adapters — PyJWT is framework-agnostic. Tagged for the de facto community stacks built on it: FastAPI's official OAuth2/JWT tutorial installs `pyjwt` and imports `jwt` directly; djangorestframework-simplejwt requires pyjwt>=1.7.1; Flask-JWT-Extended requires PyJWT>=2.11.0,<3.0.

async-api.comment: Everything is synchronous, including PyJWKClient's blocking urllib fetch — which is worth knowing in an async web app, since a JWKS refetch blocks the event loop unless run in a thread.

typed-claims.comment: Claims go in and come out as a plain dict[str, Any]; decode() is annotated to return Any. The package ships py.typed and is fully annotated, but there is no generic/model binding for custom claims — validation beyond the registered claims is the caller's job.

crypto-backend.comment: HMAC via the standard library's hmac/hashlib; all asymmetric algorithms via the optional `cryptography` package, which performs its primitives with OpenSSL.

pure-language-implementation.comment: PyJWT itself is pure Python: the only published wheel is pyjwt-2.13.0-py3-none-any.whl and the sole runtime dependency is typing_extensions (Python < 3.11). Caveat: a useful install for RS/PS/ES/EdDSA adds the `crypto` extra, and `cryptography` is a native Rust/OpenSSL extension — the default install gives you HS* and `none` only.

runs-in-browser-wasm.comment: The base package is a platform-independent pure-Python wheel with no compiled code, so it imports under any WASM-hosted CPython (Pyodide and friends). Asymmetric algorithms additionally need a WASM build of `cryptography`; that build's availability was not confirmed from a primary source in this pass, so treat HS*-only as the guaranteed subset.

edge-runtime-compatible.comment: Per the guideline, null rather than false: Cloudflare Workers / Vercel Edge / Deno Deploy are JavaScript-runtime concepts and PyJWT is a CPython library. It uses no Node built-ins and no native code in the base install, so the underlying property (portability) is captured by the browser/WASM and pure-implementation attributes instead.

fips-capable-backend.comment: Indeterminate. PyJWT delegates all asymmetric crypto to `cryptography`, whose FAQ makes no FIPS 140 statement, and PyJWT itself says nothing about FIPS. In principle a distribution-built `cryptography` linked against a system OpenSSL running its FIPS provider would inherit that validation — validation belongs to the module, not this library — but neither project documents or tests the configuration, so this is recorded as unknown rather than false.

dependency-count.comment: Default install: one direct dependency, typing_extensions>=4.0, and even that is conditional on python_version < '3.11' — so on modern Python the runtime dependency count is effectively zero. The `crypto` extra adds cryptography>=3.4.0 (which pulls cffi on most platforms). Checked 2026-07-30 against 2.13.0.

package-size.comment: pyjwt-2.13.0-py3-none-any.whl as reported by PyPI (31.3 kB); the sdist is 107,515 bytes. Excludes the optional `cryptography` dependency, which is orders of magnitude larger.

downloads.comment: PyPI downloads for the last 30 days as reported by pypistats on 2026-07-30 (last_week 162,566,972; last_day 26,707,187). PyPI counts include mirrors and CI traffic, so treat this as a within-Python-ecosystem ranking signal only.

maintenance-status.comment: Four releases in the last twelve months (2.11.0 Jan 2026, 2.12.0/2.12.1 Mar 2026, 2.13.0 May 2026), commits through 2026-07-27, and same-cycle turnaround on the 2026 advisories.

bus-factor.comment: Of the last 50 commits (checked 2026-07-30): jpadilla 17, kurtmckee 14, tamird 4, plus single contributions and 12 bot commits (pre-commit.ci, dependabot). Two humans carry the bulk of the work; the project is under the personal jpadilla account, with Auth0 as a README sponsor rather than an owner.

maturity.comment: On PyPI since 2011, classifier "Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable", the default JWT library across the Python ecosystem, and a documented process for handling advisories. Judgement call against "stable": the version is still 2.x rather than 3.0 and the 2026 advisory batch shows the security surface is still moving, but a decade and a half of broad production use plus prompt, well-documented fixes matches the guideline's "mature" bar.

rfc-conformance-testing.comment: The suite (test_algorithms, test_api_jws, test_api_jwt, test_api_jwk, test_jwks_client, plus a dedicated test_advisory.py regression file) runs against the project's own generated key fixtures in tests/keys. No RFC 7520 cookbook vectors, Wycheproof corpus or cross-implementation interop suite was found in the repository.

documentation-quality.comment: Level 4: a readthedocs site with runnable examples for HS256, RS256, PS256, ES256 and EdDSA, every registered claim, leeway, required claims, key-length validation, reading claims/headers without verification, PyJWKClient JWKS retrieval and an OIDC login walk-through, alongside an API reference. Short of 5 because there is no consolidated security-considerations chapter (guidance is scattered) and features such as detached payloads and b64=false are undocumented outside the changelog.
